title: The indirect effects of social anxiety and social support on alcohol use among UK university students: The role of negative reinforcement
abstract: Background Socially anxious students may be vulnerable to risky alcohol use, whereas perceived social support may be protective; however, the mechanisms through which social anxiety heightens risk and perceived social support reduces risk remain unclear. This study examined how social anxiety and perceived social support influence risky alcohol use through negative-reinforcement pathways of coping and conformity drinking motives. Method A convenience sample of undergraduate students from a large university in the United Kingdom ( N = 152; 74% female) completed an online self-report survey assessing perceived social support (MSPSS), social anxiety (SIAS), drinking motives (DMQ-R), and past-year alcohol use (AUDIT-C score). Using a cross-sectional observational design, structural equation modelling was conducted to test direct and indirect associations among study variables. Results Social anxiety significantly predicted coping (β = .260, p = .001) and conformity (β = .222, p = .006) motives. Past-year alcohol use was predicted by coping motives (β = .429, p < .001), but not by conformity motives. An indirect effect of social anxiety on alcohol use via coping motives was identified (β = .113, p = .005). Perceived social support was associated with lower coping motives (β = –.172, p = .038), but not with conformity motives. A protective indirect effect of perceived social support on alcohol use via lowered endorsement of coping motives was also observed (β = –.074, p = .037). Conclusion The findings suggest that social anxiety may increase risky alcohol use through coping motives, whereas perceived social support may protect against risky alcohol use by reducing coping-motivated drinking, thereby partially counteracting this risk pathway.
